chapterNote: Esther steps uninvited into the throne room and lives — the scepter is held out, favor arrives again at the knife's edge. Yet she does not blurt her request; she lays a careful table and asks only for a second banquet, buying the one night the story needs. Meanwhile Haman rides home swollen with honor and choking on a single Jew's refusal, and lets his wife and friends talk him into a gallows seventy-five feet high. Pride builds the very scaffold it will hang on.

1.text: On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the palace, facing the king's hall. The king was seated on his royal throne in the hall, facing the entrance.
1.notes: 'On the third day' — after the fast of 4:16. Esther walks into the space where being unsummoned means death, dressed as queen, staking everything on a favor she cannot command.

2.text: When the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won his favor, and he held out to her the golden scepter in his hand. So Esther came forward and touched the tip of the scepter.
2.notes: The scepter extended is life granted. The narrator simply says she 'won favor' — the same quiet, decisive grace that has carried her from the harem to the crown now spares her at the throne.

3.text: "What is it, Queen Esther?" the king asked. "What is your request? Even to half the kingdom, it will be given you."

4.text: "If it please the king," Esther answered, "let the king and Haman come today to a banquet I have prepared for him."

5.text: "Bring Haman quickly," the king said, "so that we may do as Esther asks." So the king and Haman came to the banquet Esther had prepared.

6.text: As they drank their wine, the king said to Esther, "What is your petition? It will be granted. What is your request? Even to half the kingdom, it will be done."

7.text: Esther answered, "My petition and my request is this:

8.text: if I have found favor in the king's eyes, and if it please the king to grant my petition and fulfill my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet I will prepare for them; and tomorrow I will do as the king has said."
8.notes: Esther delays. Whether wisdom, prayerful timing, or a reading of the moment, the postponed second banquet opens the gap into which the sleepless night, the reading of the chronicles, and Mordecai's honoring all fall. Her patience gives providence its room to work.

9.text: Haman went out that day glad and light of heart. But when he saw Mordecai at the king's gate, and that he neither rose nor trembled before him, Haman was filled with fury against him.

10.text: Yet Haman held himself in and went home. He sent for his friends and his wife Zeresh,

11.text: and recounted to them the splendor of his riches, his many sons, and every way the king had honored him and lifted him above the officials and servants of the king.

12.text: "What is more," Haman said, "Queen Esther let no one but me come with the king to the banquet she gave, and tomorrow I am again her invited guest, along with the king.

13.text: But all of this means nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate."
13.notes: The confession of an envious heart: every honor the empire can give is emptied out by one man who will not bow. Pride can never be fed enough; a single withheld tribute spoils the whole feast. It is this hunger that talks Haman onto his own gallows.

14.text: Then his wife Zeresh and all his friends said to him, "Have a gallows made, fifty cubits high — some seventy-five feet — and in the morning ask the king to have Mordecai hanged on it; then go with the king to the banquet in good cheer." The idea pleased Haman, and he had the gallows made.
14.amp: let a gallows [ets (H6086) — a tree, a wooden pole for impaling or hanging] be made fifty cubits high.
14.notes: An absurd height — a gallows to tower over the city, so all would see the Jew destroyed. Haman builds it the night before the very morning the king will command him to honor Mordecai instead; the instrument of his malice is finished just in time to become the instrument of his end (7:10).
